definitions: A point is a pair of integers, the origin is o = (0,0), and for every natural p, including zero, a point u can reach a point z precisely when each coordinate of z − u lies inclusively between −p and p. This condition is decidable; staying still always satisfies it, and for p = 0 it holds exactly when u = z. For any finite point list h and any point z, firstReachable(p,h,z) is the zero-based index of the first entry of h that can reach z, or the length of h if no such entry exists; in particular it is zero on the empty list. The list reducedJourney(p,h) is defined for every finite list h as follows. On the empty list it returns the empty list. On a nonempty list, let z be its last entry; if z = o, return [o], regardless of the earlier entries. Otherwise remove the last entry to obtain prior, and let i be the first index in prior of an entry that can reach z. If such an entry exists, recursively apply reducedJourney with the same p to the prefix of prior containing its first i + 1 entries, and then append z. If no such entry exists, return [z]. At each recursive call the prefix is strictly shorter than the preceding input, and the first reachable entry is selected from that call's unreduced prior list. The last-entry operation has o as its empty-list default, but the initial empty-list branch prevents that default from affecting a nonempty branch. Thus a singleton always returns itself, a list ending at o returns [o] even when it does not start at o, and a list ending away from o with no reachable preceding entry returns its non-origin endpoint alone; the definition requires neither that its input start at o nor that consecutive entries be reachable. A journey of power p means a nonempty finite list whose first entry is o and whose every pair of consecutive entries satisfies the stated coordinate bounds; indices for which one of the two entries is absent impose no condition, a singleton [o] is a journey, repetitions are allowed, and at p = 0 every entry of a journey equals o.
theorem: For every natural number p, including zero, and every finite list h of integer-pair points, assume that h is nonempty, begins at o = (0,0), and each coordinate changes by at most p in absolute value between every pair of consecutive entries. Define R on finite lists using this same p: R([]) = []; if a nonempty list ends at o, set its value to [o]; otherwise let z be its endpoint and search the list with its last entry removed for the earliest entry from which each coordinate of z differs by at most p in absolute value. If such an entry has zero-based index i, take the prefix through that entry, apply R recursively to that prefix, and append z; if no such entry exists, return [z]. The assertion is that R(h) is nonempty, begins at o, and each coordinate changes by at most p in absolute value between every pair of consecutive entries of R(h). The recursive function is total, including the empty-input and no-reachable-predecessor cases, but the hypothesis excludes an empty h. Singleton origin inputs are allowed, repetitions and zero-length jumps are allowed, and p = 0 forces all entries of h to equal o, in which case R(h) = [o]. The assertion is preservation of these journey conditions; it does not state that every list satisfying them is returned unchanged or that the returned list has a minimal length.
